The regulation requires that FD&C aluminum lakes for cosmetics be prepared by extending a certified water-soluble straight color on an alumina substratum, and each such lake must meet specific composition and specification criteria, including limits on soluble chlorides and sulfates and inorganic matter. The name of the lake is determined by combining the listed name of the parent color with the name of the basic radical (aluminum) and appending the word “Lake.” These lakes are considered straight colors and must conform to specifications set forth for the parent color, including those in §82.50.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(1) [1] requires that any aluminum lake be made by extending a salt derived from one of the certified water-soluble straight colors on an alumina substratum using either the aluminum or calcium basic radical.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(2) [2] specifies that lakes must be prepared from previously certified colors listed in this subpart, and further limits soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) to not more than 2.0 percent; insoluble HCl and inorganic matter are limited to not more than 0.5 percent [3].

21 CFR 82.51(b) [4] establishes that each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) shall be considered a straight color and listed under a name formed according to specific rules.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(1) [5] requires the name of the lake to include the listed name of the parent color from which it is prepared.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(2) [6] requires the inclusion of the name of the basic radical (aluminum or calcium) combined in the color.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(3) [7] and [8] require that the word “Lake” be appended to the name, as illustrated by the example: FD&C Blue No. 1—Aluminum Lake.

21 CFR 82.50 [9] requires a batch of a straight color (including lakes) to be certified for use in food, drugs, and cosmetics if it conforms to §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for that color.
